title: Climate Change Is Reducing Water Levels of Australia’s Murray River While Adversely Affecting Communities and Ecosystems
content: The Murray River is Australia’s longest and most important river. It is the dominant river supporting the Murray-Darling-Basin (MDB), known as Australia’s ‘food bowl’. However, the Murray River has long experienced environmental destruction from low flows, due largely to excessive irrigation.  Since the 1990s, the Murray River has further deteriorated under accelerated climate change, generating over 30 years of mostly dry or drought conditions, interspersed with floods.  Here, we analyze annual Murray River level time series at two locations, Doctors Point (Upper Murray) and Waikerie (Lower Murray), to assess the significance of climate change impacts on Murray River levels. Minimal water extraction occurs in the Upper Murray, unlike water extraction water for irrigation in the Lower Murray. The period 1960–2025 is divided into two sub-periods, 1960–1990 and 1990–2025, in which the 1990s represents the transition from the IPCC designated pre- and present-accelerated climate change. Welch’s t-test is used on the time-lagged data to determine the statistical significance of the difference in means. We found a significant decreasing river level trend in the Upper Murray, and a smaller decreasing trend in the Lower Murray, where river level management ensures they never drop below 6m.  Climate change, especially since the 1990s, created major Australian region atmospheric circulation changes, with reduced annual and cool season (April to October) rainfall.  Decreased river levels negate water management efforts; hence action is urgently needed. However, growing water demand in the arid Lower Murray will negatively impact ecosystems and diminish agricultural water availability.
